c4.container.body: The separately deployable pieces and the technology each one is — that is what the brackets are for. Note what the definition does NOT say: nothing about Docker. The word predates it, and a database schema is a container here.
c4.container.quote: A container is an application or a data store. For example, a server-side web application, a client-side single-page application, a desktop application, a mobile app, a database schema, a folder on a file system, an Amazon Web Services S3 bucket, etc.
c4.container.title: Level 2 — Container
c4.context.audience: Everybody, both technical and non-technical people, inside and outside the software development team
c4.context.body: One box for the whole platform, the people who use it, and the systems it exchanges with. No technology at all — this is the level you can put in front of someone who does not write software.
c4.context.quote: A system context diagram is a good starting point for diagramming and documenting a software system, allowing you to step back and see the big picture. … Detail isn't important here as this is your zoomed out view showing a big picture.
c4.context.title: Level 1 — System Context
c4.hierarchy: A software system is made up of one or more containers (applications and data stores), each of which contains one or more components, which in turn are implemented by one or more code elements (classes, interfaces, objects, functions, etc).
c4.hierarchyNote: The hierarchy is the model. The diagrams are just four ways of looking at it, and C4 is deliberately notation independent and tooling independent — the boxes here could be drawn any way at all without ceasing to be C4.
c4.lede: Four levels of zoom over one static structure. The definitions below are quoted from c4model.com rather than paraphrased, because the value of a shared notation is that everyone is using the same one. Every diagram here is rendered from Mermaid source held in the page.
c4.supplementary: Beyond these four, C4 names a set of supporting diagrams — system landscape, dynamic, and deployment. The request flow on the other tab is the dynamic one; deployment is described in the platform note below rather than drawn, because this system runs in a single environment.
c4.title: The C4 model, as its author defines it
catalog.campaign-service.what: The Campaign Cohort Hub. It segments customers into cohorts from booking history and accrued TEU, decides which offer each cohort should see, and emits targeting events. It reads from the Data Platform rather than the transactional store, so audience work can never slow down booking.
catalog.campaign-service.when: A lane is running under capacity for the next sailing window. The hub identifies customers who shipped that corridor in the last two quarters but not this one, and targets a time-boxed incentive at exactly that cohort instead of discounting the lane for everyone.
catalog.data-platform.what: The relational analytics store. Booking and quotation events land here from the Legacy ERP Engine on a read replica, separated from the transactional primary so reporting load can never contend with booking writes.
catalog.data-platform.when: The Lead Product Owner (LPO) needs monthly TEU accrual per customer to check that Volume Loyalty Framework milestones are firing correctly. That query scans a quarter of history — running it against the transactional primary would put booking latency at risk, so it runs here instead.
catalog.feature-flags.what: A managed flag evaluation service. It decouples deploying code from releasing behaviour: a change ships dark, is switched on for a named slice of traffic, and can be switched off in seconds without a rollback, a redeploy, or a release window.
catalog.feature-flags.when: Rolling the Quotation Flex Cart multi-port hold out to the first 5% of Silver Sail customers. If rate-reservation latency against the Legacy ERP Engine degrades under the added load, the flag is killed immediately — the code stays deployed and nobody has to page a release engineer.
catalog.quotation-service.what: The Core Quotation Module. It resolves a lane to a base rate, converts cargo volume into container units, applies the type multiplier and surcharges, asks the Volume Loyalty Framework for the customer's discount, and reserves the resulting rate against the Legacy ERP Engine for a fixed validity window.
catalog.quotation-service.when: A customer requests a rate at 02:00 local time, outside any human desk's hours. The service prices the lane, holds it for 72 hours through the Quotation Flex Cart, and the customer books the next morning at the same number — no re-quote, no negotiation, no staff involved.
catalog.routing-gateway.what: A layer-7 reverse proxy sitting in front of every service. It terminates TLS, enforces per-client rate limits, routes by path prefix, injects a trace header so one request can be followed end to end, and load-balances across replicas. It is also the cluster ingress.
catalog.routing-gateway.when: The Campaign Cohort Hub launches a promotion and quote traffic spikes roughly eightfold within a minute. The gateway absorbs the burst, throttles the clients that are hammering the endpoint, and shifts traffic across healthy replicas — with no service redeploy and no code change.
catalog.translation-api.what: Lokalise, the managed localisation platform this site actually runs on. Translation keys live outside the application build, so copy is corrected in any locale without shipping a release. `scripts/pull-locales.mjs` writes the bundles before the build and the app imports them, so the running site has no runtime token and no network dependency on a translation vendor. Any key missing from a locale falls back to the base rather than rendering blank.
catalog.translation-api.when: A surcharge label reads ambiguously in one market and the local team wants it reworded before the next sailing. They edit the string in the platform, the next build picks it up, and no engineer touches the repository.
catalog.web-portal.what: The customer-facing application. It renders quotation forms and rate comparisons on the server, hydrates only the interactive parts, and holds no business rules of its own — pricing and eligibility always come from the service layer so a browser can never be the source of truth.
catalog.web-portal.when: A customer opens a rate search from a slow mobile connection in a port city. Server rendering means the first meaningful paint carries real lane data rather than a spinner, and the interactive quote form hydrates afterwards without blocking the read.

home.expertise.body: Port to port. A single quotation fixes a slot, a rate and a sailing date for 72 hours, and the booking, the filings and the delivery window are all bound to it. This portfolio takes that one transaction apart — the pricing, the services behind it, and the way the work itself is organised.

node.analytics.role: Reporting over the Data Platform replica. Read-only, and deliberately downstream of everything.
node.api-integration.role: A partner system posts straight to the API. Same contract, same validation, no human keying.
node.campaign-service.role: Segments customers and targets offers. The Campaign Cohort Hub.
node.data-platform.role: The analytics store, fed from a read replica so reporting can never contend with booking writes.
node.email.role: A request arrives as free text and is parsed into the same intake payload, so nothing downstream ever learns which channel it came from.
node.erp-system.role: The Legacy ERP Engine. System of record for rates, bookings and reservations: everything transactional is ultimately true here or not true at all.
node.feature-flags.role: Decides which behaviour a given customer sees, so deploying and releasing stop being the same event.
node.new-request.role: A customer starts a rate request in the portal. The default entry point, and the one every other channel converges on.
node.notification-service.role: Fans the outcome out asynchronously, so a slow mail provider can never delay a quote response.
node.quotation-service.role: Prices a lane and reserves the resulting rate. The Core Quotation Module.
node.request-intake.role: Captures and normalises the request, whatever channel it arrived on, and hands one shape to the service layer.
node.request-tracker.role: The customer-facing status view. It reads request state; it never mutates it.
node.routing-gateway.role: The single front door. Everything the platform serves passes through here and is routed, rate-limited and traced.
node.translation-api.role: Supplies localised copy from outside the build, so wording can be corrected without a release.
node.validation.role: Schema, lane and eligibility checks run before anything is priced. A request that fails here never reaches the service layer.

The Quotation Service scales horizontally on p95 latency rather than CPU, because a slow rate reservation against the Legacy ERP Engine shows up as latency long before it shows up as load.

process.ai.title: AI-driven agile (automated)
process.chart.caption: Story points across the bottom, lead time in days up the side. The dashed line with square markers is traditional; the solid crimson line is AI-driven.
process.chart.table: Read the figures as a table
process.chart.title: The bigger the batch, the wider the gap.
process.forward.lede: The same agile principles, with the queues taken out. The one human step that remains is the judgement call.
process.lede: The work is not slow. What differs between these two teams is how long the work spends waiting, not how fast anybody types.
process.outcome.alt: A team at a planning board, work on the wall behind them.
process.outcome.caveat: Every constant is in processModel.ts with the reason for it beside it, and none of them was measured. They were chosen to produce a curve, which is the honest description of what they are. The 3D simulation, the chart and the bars all read that same file, so they agree with each other and with nothing else.
process.outcome.lede: Below is a queueing model, not a measurement. It exists to show one mechanism: hands-on effort grows in line with batch size and queue wait grows faster than it, so the gap widens as the batch grows. At {sp} story points the model puts the ratio at {ratio}×. Read that number as an illustration of the shape. The measured findings are in the section above it, and they are smaller.
process.outcome.title: The same work, and where the time actually goes
process.protocol.approvalsBody: A pull request needs at least two independent approvals. One reviewer is both a bottleneck and a single point of failure; branch protection enforces the count, and a green build alone never unlocks the merge.
process.protocol.branchesBody: Branch names carry their type and ticket, so the board and the repository can be reconciled without anybody maintaining a mapping by hand.
process.protocol.commitBody: Every commit opens with its ticket id. Release notes and the audit trail are generated from that tag, and a pre-receive hook rejects any subject line without one — the convention is enforced by the repository, not by reviewer goodwill.
process.protocol.lede: None of these depend on anybody remembering them, which is the only reason they hold under load.
process.protocol.title: Three rules, enforced by tooling.
process.sim.lede: The same five steps, laid out twice. Drag a story point onto a desk and watch where it stops — the queues are the argument, and they are there before you touch anything.
process.sim.title: Drop work into either room.
process.trad.blurb: People build. Work waits between steps.
process.trad.title: Traditional scrum (AI assisted)
process.two.lede: People build in both. The difference is how the work moves between them.
process.two.title: Same work. Different flow.
process.why.gatesBody: A pull request needs two independent approvals, so it waits on two calendars rather than one.
process.why.handoffsBody: Work is passed from one person to the next, and a queue forms at every boundary.
process.why.stagesBody: Each stage handles one item at a time, so a second item cannot flow in parallel — it queues.
process.why.title: Work waits because of the process, not the people.
quality.attr.post: . {note} Published studies put the same two effects at {pubSpeed}× and {pubDefect}× —
quality.body1: Automated review does not make the code better — the same {written} defects per thousand lines are written either way. It changes how many get out, catching {recovery}% at the gate.
quality.body2: At a {factor}× injection rate the gate has to catch {breakEven}% just to break even with writing the code by hand. The best measured AI reviewer catches {recovery}%. So “add AI review” is not a conclusion — it is a target with a number on it, and we are {short} points short of it.
quality.gap.body: The internal report has two numbers in it: throughput ×{speed} and defects ×{defects}. It does not have a third. Nobody measured what the automated review actually caught on our own delivery, so the claim that it closes the gap rests entirely on other people's catch rates — {recovery}% at the best measured gate — applied to our injection rate. That arithmetic is in the cards above and it is the weakest thing on this page. The measurement that would settle it is one we did not take.
quality.gap.title: What we cannot show you
quality.internal.label: OTSV internal report
quality.internal.methodology: Throughput and defect counts taken from the team's own delivery record. Sample size and counting method are not published, so this figure cannot be reproduced from outside — which is exactly why the published studies sit beside it.
quality.internal.note: Measured on our own delivery, not published.
quality.lede: Assistance did not make the team a little faster and a little sloppier. It roughly tripled what got written and roughly quintupled what was wrong with it — and the second number is the one that decides whether the first one was worth having.
quality.modal.caption: The measurements these figures come from
quality.modal.lede: No published study reports anything close to our own numbers. The internal figure is {speedGap}× the published median on throughput and {defectGap}× on defects. That gap is worth sitting with rather than explaining away: either the team is unusual, or the counting is — and the honest position is that a figure nobody outside can reproduce is weaker evidence than one measured across 84 organisations, however much we trust our own.
quality.modal.title: What everyone else found

quiz.announceCorrect: Correct. The explanation is below, and the next question is ready.
quiz.announceWrong: Not quite. The correct answer is {text}. The explanation is below.
quiz.full: Full marks. Every rule above is enforced by tooling rather than by memory, which is the point.
quiz.lede: Five questions on the rules the delivery model actually runs on. Each one explains why the rule exists, not just what it is.
quiz.q1.c: The branch name repeated as the subject line
quiz.q1.prompt: Under the Agile Delivery Protocol, which commit message structure is mandatory?
quiz.q1.why: Every commit stays traceable to a ticket. Release notes and audit trails are generated from the tag, and the pre-receive hook rejects any subject line that does not open with the ticket id — so the convention is enforced by the repository, not by reviewer goodwill.
quiz.q2.prompt: At what TEU milestone interval does a Blue Wave customer earn a performance reward?
quiz.q2.why: Blue Wave is the entry tier and carries no rate discount at all — its entire value is the coupon granted every 5 TEUs of accrued volume. Get the interval wrong and the whole entry-tier incentive is mispriced.
quiz.q3.c: None, provided the build is green
quiz.q3.prompt: How many peer approvals must a Pull Request carry before it can be merged?
quiz.q3.why: The Agile Delivery Protocol requires at least two independent approvals so that no single reviewer becomes a bottleneck or a single point of failure. Branch protection enforces it; a green build alone never unlocks the merge.
quiz.q4.c: One cubic metre of cargo volume
quiz.q4.prompt: In ocean freight capacity, what does one TEU represent?
quiz.q4.why: TEU is the normalising unit for the entire Volume Loyalty Framework. A 40' High Cube counts as 2 TEU, so five of them accrue 10 TEU rather than 5 — misreading this doubles or halves every reward calculation downstream.
quiz.q5.a: Issuing the final bill of lading
quiz.q5.c: Holding short-term freight rates across multiple ports so a customer can compare and book later
quiz.q5.d: Persisting booking records in the Legacy ERP Engine
quiz.q5.prompt: What is the Quotation Flex Cart responsible for?
quiz.q5.why: The Quotation Flex Cart is a rate-hold layer, not a booking system. It keeps quotes valid for a fixed window across several lanes; the transaction is only committed once the Legacy ERP Engine confirms the booking.
quiz.review: Review the ones you missed below. Each explanation says why the rule exists, not just what it is.
quiz.title: Knowledge check.

sim.readout.caption: Simulated cycle time in days for each dropped work item under both delivery approaches.
sim.readout.empty: Drop a story point box onto a step, or select one and press Enter, to see how long the same work takes under each approach.
sim.readout.note1: Flow efficiency under Traditional Agile is the share of elapsed time that is actual work. It falls as batch size grows, because queue wait is superlinear in story points while hands-on effort is linear.
sim.readout.note2: These are modelled figures, not measurements. The assumption doing most of the work is that AI-driven delivery carries no approval queue: hands-on effort is comparable, and almost the entire difference is wait time that never accrues. If your review gate stays human, the gap narrows sharply — which is the argument for removing the gate, not for the tooling alone.

station.analysis.does.ai-driven: Proposes criteria and a size; a person confirms or overrides it.
station.analysis.does.traditional: Works out acceptance criteria and sizes the item, then hands it on.
station.deploy.does.ai-driven: Ships and watches the result. There is no approval queue to join.
station.deploy.does.traditional: Cuts the release — but only after two reviewers free up to approve it.
station.dev.does.ai-driven: A person sets the intent; generation and commit formatting are automatic.
station.dev.does.traditional: Writes the code, then hand-formats the commit to the [Ticket_ID] tag.
station.intake.does.ai-driven: Drafts the ticket from the request and routes it to the right lane on its own.
station.intake.does.traditional: Reads the request, writes the ticket by hand, and drops it on the next queue.
station.test.does.ai-driven: Runs checks and reviews the diff continuously, in-line, as work arrives.
station.test.does.traditional: Runs the checks by hand and re-reads the diff line by line.
